Part 0 · Opening
Writing Architecture Documentation with arc42

A one-day beginner workshop

By 17:00 you will have a first-draft arc42 for a real system and a method you can reuse.

Part 0 · Opening

Why we need this

  • Knowledge lives in heads. Newcomers wait for someone to explain.
  • Decisions are forgotten. Teams re-debate old choices or break them by accident.
  • Qualities go unstated. “Fast” and “secure” mean different things to different people.
  • Machines are now readers. AI tools act on what is written and guess what isn’t.

Part 0 · Opening

By the end of today you can

  • Explain what software architecture and arc42 are
  • Identify stakeholders and write measurable quality goals
  • Draw a context view and a Level-1 building-block view, and write one component contract
  • Describe a runtime scenario and a deployment view
  • Record one decision as an ADR
  • Use AI to draft sections, then find and fix its mistakes

Part 0 · Opening

How we will learn

Each part follows one loop:

Why, what goes in and out, steps, worked example, try it, check.

I do, then we do, then you do.

Experienced? Try each exercise first, then compare with the example. Finished examples help most when a topic is new to you.

Basis: worked-example and expertise-reversal research (Renkl and Atkinson, 2003; Kalyuga et al., 2003).

Part 0 · Opening

Why you will spend most of today doing

  • A meta-analysis of 225 studies found that active learning raised exam performance by about 0.47 standard deviations
  • Students in traditional lectures were 1.5 times more likely to fail
  • So most of today is exercises, peer checks and discussion

Freeman et al., PNAS, 2014. Undergraduate STEM courses, not professional workshops: read it as a direction, not a guarantee.

Part 0 · Opening

How learning sticks

  • Practice testing (high utility): each part opens with recall from memory
  • Spaced practice (high): one running example returns in every section
  • Mixed practice (moderate): exercises mix goals, structure and decisions
  • Self-explanation (moderate): after an example, tell your neighbour why

Dunlosky et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013. Rereading and highlighting were rated low.

Part 0 · Opening

Rules for AI today

  1. Human draft first (Exercises 1–11)
  2. AI second: ask it why and what’s missing, not only “write it”
  3. You decide: every AI line gets a human verdict
In a randomized trial of 52 mostly junior engineers learning a new library, AI assistance lowered quiz scores by about 17 points. Those who asked conceptual questions did far better than those who delegated the code.

Shen and Tamkin, Anthropic, January 2026. A single small study; treat it as a signal, not a verdict.

Part 0 · Opening

Form teams, choose your case

  • Teams of 3–4
  • Pick one system your team can explain from memory

School library lending · Clinic appointment booking · Maxi-taxi arrival tracker · Community fundraising platform · Your own

Write on your team card: system name, one-sentence purpose, three likely users.

Part 0 · Opening

Set up (5 min)

  1. Create arc42-team.md
  2. Paste the skeleton from the student guide
  3. Paste the Mermaid sample and confirm it renders
  4. Share the file with your team

Then take the baseline quiz: 8 questions, ungraded. You’ll retake it at the end.

notes: Ask: which of these have you lived through?

Novices learn well from finished examples with support that fades as they gain skill. For people with prior knowledge the same examples can slow learning (the expertise reversal effect), so invite experienced participants to attempt first. A rough but complete skeleton beats a polished but partial one.
Effect size 0.47 SD on exams and concept inventories; failure rates 21.8% under active learning versus 33.8% under lecturing (an odds ratio of 1.95).

Dunlosky and colleagues rated ten techniques. Practice testing and distributed practice came out as high utility. Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation were moderate. Summarising, highlighting and rereading were low.

Anthropic funded and ran the study. It covered one Python library and short tasks. Participants who asked conceptual questions scored well; those who delegated generation scored poorly. Full study: anthropic.com/research/AI-assistance-coding-skills
Doubles-to-Go is reserved as the facilitator’s worked example; teams should choose a different system.
Any Markdown editor with Mermaid preview, a repository or a shared doc works.
